entry.author: NZ Law Commission
entry.summary:
On 23 June 2026, Te Aka Matua o te Ture | Law Commission submitted its report to the Minister to complete its review of hate crime law. The report was presented to Parliament on 22 July 2026. 

The Law Commission was asked by the Government to review the law relating to hate crime, with a focus on whether the law should be changed to create standalone hate crime offences. 

We concluded that the current legal model, which takes hostile motivation into account at sentencing, remains the most appropriate model compared to alternatives.

Our report makes 12 recommendations to ensure hate crimes are consistently identified, recorded and denounced by the justice system.
Key recommendations include:
• Creating a ‘hate crime flag’ in the courts. This would allow Police to record an allegation that an offence was motivated by hostility when charging a defendant, prompting judges to address it at bail and sentencing hearings. Judges would also be required to formally record the application of the hostility aggravating factor on the court record.
• Requiring judges to expressly state in their sentencing decisions when they find hostility was a motivating factor, so that the nature and seriousness of the offending is communicated to the public and the offender.
• Amending the Sentencing Act 2002 to ensure the aggravating factor can apply if a victim is targeted because of their association with an affected group, even if they are not a member of that group (for example, a family member or support person), or is an innocent bystander (for example, the owner of public-facing property vandalised to spread hateful messages).
• Adding ‘sex’ to the list of characteristics covered by the aggravating factor in the Sentencing Act. This would clarify that offending motivated by hostility based on sex, particularly hostility towards women, is a hate crime.
• Providing guidance and training for Police, prosecutors and judges on any changes to the law, and publishing data annually on hostility-motivated offending.
